newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine nuclear body presents plan to reopen reactor.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine nuclear body presents plan to reopen reactor.

text.p: Ukrainian nuclear authorities have prepared contingency plans to restart one of the three remaining reactors at the Chernobyl power plant, officials said on Thursday.
The plant is due to be closed down entirely in 2000 under a deal with the west.
Restarting the Number Two reactor, shut down for the past five years, would take the place of reactor Number One which is to close on November 30 in line as part the deal.

"Technical documents have been prepared and sent to the government for approval or otherwise. You could say they have been prepared just in case," Valery Idelson, press spokesman on Chernobyl based in the Ukrainian capital, told Reuters.
Two reactors -- One and Three -- are still working at Chernobyl, where the fourth reactor blew up in 1986 and spewed a radioactive cloud across much of Europe.
The second reactor was stopped in 1991 after a fire in its control room.
Kiev has agreed to shut down the entire plant by 2000 in return for $3.1 billion in grants and credits from the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations.
But Ukrainian authorities have complained that the process of getting cash from its Western partners has been too slow.
"We have no guarantees (from the West) and we don't have the money yet either," Idelson said.
The former Soviet republic has payments problems not seen in rich nations, and the two remaining reactors have been supplying its 52 million people with five percent of their electricity.

But Idelson stressed that any decision on reopening the reactor -- a move which one Western analyst said would have a very detrimental effect on relations with Ukraine -- would only be taken by the country's leadership.
"If the decision is taken, it would be taken not only by the government, but by the president himself. It is not just an economic issue, but a political one," Idelson said.
He added that reactor Number Two would not be restarted for at least a year if such a decision was taken.
Mykhailo Bohdanov, press aide to Chernobyl's director, told Reuters that discussions had taken place at the plant about a month ago about technical issues of reopening the reactor.
He could not say exactly when the papers were passed on to the government, but he estimated it was in the last two weeks.
A spokeswoman for Derzhkomatom, the state nuclear authority which prepared the papers, said there had been no reaction from Western partners, since no decision had been taken yet.
But one Western nuclear expert who asked not to be named said that even thinking about reopening the reactor was potentially harmful for Ukraine's relationship with the West.

Asked if preparing such documents could affect the bond of trust between the two sides, he said: "It's getting pretty close...If Ukraine really took this step it would represent a severe setback in the relationship."
The Chernobyl aid deal foresees Ukraine cutting its wasteful energy consumption through measures such as gas meters.
